You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis

Details:
The failing test case tests that the input string containing a supplementary plane Unicode character ("\ud842\udfb7") followed by "A" is unchanged by the method StringEscapeUtils.escapeXml. According to the test, since there are no XML special characters in the input, the output of escapeXml(input) should match the input exactly.

From the code snippets, we observe the following call flow:

- StringEscapeUtils.escapeXml(String input) calls ESCAPE_XML.translate(input).
- ESCAPE_XML is an AggregateTranslator composed of LookupTranslators for XML basic and apostrophe escapes.
- The CharSequenceTranslator.translate(CharSequence) method iterates over the input string by Unicode code points (calls Character.codePointCount and processes accordingly).
- Within the loop for each code point at position `pos`, it calls translate(input, pos, out) (an abstract method implemented by LookupTranslator).
- LookupTranslator.translate(CharSequence, int, Writer) attempts to greedily match subsequences of the input, looking up matching strings in a lookup map holding character-to-escaped-sequence mappings.
- If no match is found, the input character(s) for the current code point are written out unmodified.

The bug arises because LookupTranslator performs its matching and lookup based on sequences of char values (UTF-16 code units) in the input string, but supplementary Unicode characters (those above U+FFFF, such as the one in the test input) are represented as surrogate pairs in UTF-16, spanning two char positions.

In the translate(CharSequence, int, Writer) method of LookupTranslator, the check for matching sequences does not appear to properly handle surrogate pairs or supplementary characters. Specifically, the method looks up subSequences of the input string, but the input.subSequence call is based on char indexes, not code point indexes. The indexing assumes that each character is one char, but supplementary characters are two chars (surrogate pairs) and should be treated as a single code point.

Because of this discrepancy, when the input contains supplementary plane characters, LookupTranslator may misinterpret surrogate pairs as separate chars or separate sequences, which leads to incorrect or unexpected escaping output (or double escaping). This results in the output not matching the input, even though the input contained no characters that should be escaped for XML.

In summary, the fault lies in the LookupTranslator.translate method's treatment of input subsequences by char indexes instead of proper code point aware indexing. It does not correctly handle supplementary characters represented by surrogate pairs, leading to incorrect escaping results when input contains such characters.

The other recent bug reports are unrelated (documentation fixes or build warnings) and do not affect this diagnosis.

This diagnosis matches the issue described: the method outputs wrong results for supplementary plane characters because it does not handle surrogate pairs correctly in its lookup and escaping.

Recommended fix would be to make LookupTranslator and related escaping logic properly handle supplementary characters by using codepoint-aware indexing and matching. 

This concludes the diagnosis.
